Prevalent

/PREV-uh-luhnt/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prevalent means widespread; existing or occurring frequently in a particular place or at a particular time.

Prevalent means widespread — existing or occurring frequently in a particular place or time. Smartphones are so prevalent among teenagers that a classroom without them feels strange.

Worked Example

Before vaccines existed, measles was prevalent in nearly every town, infecting most children before age ten.

Measles wasn't just present — it occurred frequently, almost everywhere, at that time. Prevalent describes exactly that pattern: commonly found throughout a place or period.

How Prevalent Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

widespread

widespread: found or happening over a large area or among many people

common

common: occurring often; ordinary

pervasive

pervasive: spreading through every part of something

Antonyms

rare

rare: seldom found or occurring

scarce

scarce: existing in amounts too small to meet demand

How Strong Is It? — common → prevalent → ubiquitous

common vs. prevalent

common vs. prevalent: Common is weaker — it just means something happens often; prevalent adds the sense that it dominates a particular place or time.

ubiquitous vs. prevalent

ubiquitous vs. prevalent: Ubiquitous is stronger — it claims something is found absolutely everywhere at once, while prevalent means widespread within a specific setting.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before, in advance (Latin prae-)

Root — val

Root — val: to be strong, to have power (Latin valere)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: in a state of; -ing (adjective ending)

Put it together

Put it together: Pre- ('before, ahead of') + valere ('to be strong') builds Latin praevalere — 'to be stronger than the rest, to win out.' What is prevalent has out-muscled the alternatives, strength 'ahead of' everything else, and now shows up everywhere in that place or time.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / academic

Prevalent usually takes 'in' or 'among' ('prevalent in cities,' 'prevalent among voters') and describes conditions, practices, beliefs, or diseases that occur frequently across a group or place. It describes how often something is FOUND — not how physically large one instance of it is.
